Pakistan airspace clearance delay disrupts Rooppur uranium shipment
item.description:
Bangladesh's Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has encountered another setback after Russia delayed the scheduled delivery of nuclear fuel for its second unit, reportedly because it failed to secure timely airspace clearance from Pakistan.
The delay has raised questions about the project's commissioning schedule, particularly as Bangladesh struggles with growing electricity shortages and increased load-shedding amid fuel supply constraints.
Pakistan, however, has denied that its decision was politically motivated, describing the matter as a technical and procedural issue involving aviation regulations and diplomatic flight clearances.
In response to the delay, Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom has announced a revised delivery schedule, with shipments of nuclear fuel for the second unit expected to arrive between October and December 2026.
The latest disruption comes as the first unit of the 2,400MW nuclear power plant is already facing technical difficulties, further complicating Bangladesh's efforts to bring the long-awaited project into commercial operation.
The reported delay in securing Pakistani airspace clearance has triggered considerable debate in Bangladesh, particularly given the recent improvement in diplomatic relations between Dhaka and Islamabad.
The issue has also drawn attention on social media, with questions being raised about Pakistan's decision and its potential implications for Bangladesh's energy security.
Responding to the controversy, Pakistan's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider told BBC Urdu that the country processes requests for diplomatic flights and overflight clearances under established international procedures and civil aviation protocols.
"Pakistan remains committed to international diplomatic norms and processes all requests for diplomatic flights and overflight clearances within standard timelines, fully consistent with our established guidelines and civil aviation protocols," Haider said.
He explained that flight schedules could change because of technical and procedural requirements, including coordination among relevant aviation authorities.
"The matter relates to technical and procedural arrangements concerning flight routing and airspace clearances, which may occasionally require coordination among relevant aviation and other authorities, resulting in adjustments to flight schedules," he said.
The spokesperson also emphasized that Pakistan attaches considerable importance to its relations with Bangladesh and urged observers not to interpret the incident as a political decision.
He said the issue should be viewed in its proper technical context rather than through interpretations that could undermine bilateral relations.
However, Pakistan's statement did not provide specific details about the clearance application, the reasons for the delay or whether alternative flight routes had been considered.
Following the disruption, Rosatom announced a revised schedule for delivering nuclear fuel to the second unit of the Rooppur plant.
According to the Russian state corporation, deliveries are scheduled to begin in October 2026 and continue through December. The fuel will be transported in several flights in accordance with the project's contractual obligations and implementation schedule.
The revised timeline means that the fuel shipment originally expected in September will now arrive later than planned.
Although Rosatom confirmed the revised schedule, it did not officially identify Pakistan as the country responsible for the delay.
Nuclear fuel transportation involves stringent international safety and security requirements. Such shipments require special arrangements, including diplomatic overflight clearances from countries along the flight route.
Consequently, delays in obtaining the necessary permissions can disrupt transportation schedules.
However, the availability of alternative routes and the exact circumstances behind the delay remain unclear.
The delay in the second unit's fuel delivery comes as the first unit continues to face technical challenges.
Fuel loading at the first unit officially began in April 2026, marking a major milestone in the country's first nuclear power project.
The government had expected trial electricity generation to begin in September. However, technical problems with a key reactor component have delayed commissioning.
Bangladesh is constructing the 2,400MW Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Ishwardi, Pabna, with Russian financial and technical assistance.
The project consists of two units, each with a generation capacity of 1,200MW.
Under the original plan, the first unit was scheduled to begin commercial electricity generation in 2023.
However, the Covid-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, supply chain disruptions and complications in international financial transactions contributed to delays.
The nuclear fuel required for the first unit arrived in Bangladesh in 2023. Nevertheless, construction, testing and commissioning activities continued beyond the original deadline.
The project also faced criticism over the pace of implementation during the interim government's tenure following the political upheaval of August 5, 2024.
Although fuel loading at the first unit began in April this year, the latest technical difficulties have further complicated the commissioning process.
With the second unit's fuel delivery also delayed, the project's overall timeline has come under renewed scrutiny.
The latest setback comes at a challenging time for Bangladesh's power sector, which is struggling to meet electricity demand amid fuel shortages and financial constraints.
Reduced LNG imports and outstanding payments to private power producers have disrupted electricity generation.
As a result, load-shedding has increased in several parts of the country, putting additional pressure on households, businesses and industries.
The government has been counting on electricity from Rooppur to help ease the supply shortage and reduce dependence on expensive oil-fired power plants.
Once operational, each unit will have the capacity to generate 1,200MW of electricity, potentially adding significantly to the national grid.

item.title: Govt moves on Teesta Master Plan, feasibility study proposed
item.description:
The government has taken a fresh step toward advancing the much-discussed Teesta Master Plan, with the Ministry of Water Resources sending a Tk 23-crore proposal to the Planning Commission for a feasibility study on the project.
If approved, an international consultant will be appointed through competitive bidding to assess the technical and economic viability of the proposed interventions, including a new barrage, river training, dredging, flood control, water conservation and related infrastructure.
Water Resources Secretary Dr AKM Shahabuddin said the feasibility study would be crucial for taking the Teesta Master Plan toward implementation.
“The technical and economic viability of every component will be assessed through the study, and subsequent works for the main project will be taken based on its recommendations,” he said.
Planning Division Secretary SM Shakil Akhter said the proposal would be examined under the established procedure, taking into account the project's necessity, cost, potential benefits and feasibility.
“If approved, it will pave the way for appointing a consultant through international competitive bidding,” he told BSS.
The government has identified finding a permanent solution to the Teesta River’s problems and promoting economic transformation in the northwestern region as priorities. The BNP's 2026 election manifesto also pledged to ensure a fair share of water from the Teesta and other trans-boundary rivers, while stressing balanced regional development and greater use of the agricultural and economic potential of northern Bangladesh.
The proposed master plan envisages a broad package of river and regional development measures rather than focusing solely on a barrage.
It includes riverbank protection or river training along about 110 kilometres, dredging of another 110 kilometres of the river, and construction of 224 kilometres of flood-control embankments with roads on top.
The plan also proposes constructing or repairing 67 spurs and reclaiming and developing about 170 square kilometres of land.
Engineer Md Ruhul Amin, director general of the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), said the plan takes an integrated approach covering river-flow management, bank protection, flood control, irrigation and transport infrastructure.
The feasibility study, he said, would determine the precise locations and scope of the proposed works.
The proposed embankment-cum-road infrastructure could improve connectivity in riverside communities that are frequently cut off during the monsoon. At the same time, the embankments would provide flood protection, potentially combining two important infrastructure functions.
Dredging, however, would require careful consideration of the river’s natural behaviour. River expert Mohammad Ejaz said dredging should take into account sediment transport, water discharge and the river’s flow dynamics.
“Merely deepening the riverbed will not provide a long-term solution,” he told the national news agency adding that the feasibility study should identify appropriate dredging locations and determine how dredged sediment would be managed.
A new barrage is another major component under consideration. The government is examining the technical and financial feasibility of constructing another barrage on the Teesta to conserve water during the dry season.
According to Dr Md Ataur Rahman, a professor of Water Resources Engineering at BUET, the feasibility assessment must examine upstream and downstream flows, flood management, irrigation requirements, structural safety, maintenance and environmental considerations alongside water-storage capacity.
The Teesta is closely tied to the lives and economies of people in Rangpur, Lalmonirhat, Nilphamari, Kurigram and Gaibandha. Reduced dry-season flow affects irrigation and agriculture, while high monsoon flows contribute to flooding and river erosion, threatening homes and farmland.
Riverbank protection is therefore another key element of the plan, alongside proposals to strengthen river training and repair or construct spurs. The proposed land reclamation could also open opportunities for agriculture, infrastructure and other forms of local economic development.
Yet the scale of the eventual benefits will depend on the findings of the feasibility study, environmental assessments, final project design, financing, implementation quality and long-term maintenance.
For people in the northern region, the latest move comes after years of surveys, plans and expectations surrounding the Teesta. The proposed feasibility study does not mark the completion of the master plan, but it could move the initiative into a more concrete administrative and technical phase.
Several steps would still remain, including completion of the feasibility study and environmental assessment, finalisation of the project design, government approval, financing and field-level implementation.
If implemented, the Teesta Master Plan would extend beyond a conventional barrage or river-management project. It could bring water conservation, irrigation, flood control, erosion prevention, river training, transport, land management and regional economic development under a single integrated framework.

item.title: 5th Bay of Bengal Conversation begins in Dhaka Saturday
item.description:
The fifth edition of the international conference, the Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026, will begin in Dhaka on Saturday.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will inaugurate the three-day conference, which is being organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS) at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Dhaka.
The conference will bring together more than 200 speakers, over 300 delegates, and more than 1,000 participants from over 100 countries
Participants include former and present heads of state, ministers, diplomats, military experts, academics, researchers, journalists, business and investment leaders, human rights defenders, technology specialists, and representatives of international development organisations.
CGS President Zillur Rahman formally announced the commencement of the conference at a media exchange held at Pan Pacific Sonargaon on Friday morning.
“The Bay of Bengal is becoming increasingly important in the context of maritime security and regional geopolitics. As a vital link between South Asia and Southeast Asia, one of the key objectives of this initiative is to explore effective solutions to the challenges and opportunities rooted in the Bay,” he said.
Zillur said this year’s discussions will focus on geopolitics, security, trust, climate change, spirituality, and humanity.
He said CGS has already expanded its activities to the United States and plans to extend its presence to Brussels and Dubai in the future.
CGS Executive Director Parvez Karim Abbasi highlighted the strategic relevance of the region, saying: “The Bay of Bengal Conversation is South Asia’s largest privately organised international geopolitical conference. Over the years, it has grown in scale while continuing to bring difficult and sensitive issues to the centre of discussion.”
Also present at the media exchange were CGS Director Subir Das, Research Assistant Tasfia Rahman, and other members of CGS.

item.title: PM Tarique inaugurates fifth Bay of Bengal Conversation
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday inaugurated the fifth edition of the international forum "Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026", bringing together policymakers, diplomats, researchers and experts from over 100 countries.
The three-day conference, organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS), is being held at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Dhaka from October 3 to 5.
The prime minister formally opened the three-day event around 10am with his address to the opening session.
More than 200 speakers, over 300 delegates and more than 1,000 participants are expected to attend the forum, including former and current heads of state and government, ministers, diplomats, military experts, academics, researchers, journalists, business and investment leaders, human rights defenders, technology specialists and representatives of international development organisations.
Former Serbian President Boris Tadić and former Malian Prime Minister Moussa Mara are among the notable participants.
The theme of this year’s conference is “Fragments, Frontiers and Futures”, with the tagline “Navigating Power, Technology and Trust in a World Rewritten.”
The discussions will focus on major regional and global issues, including geopolitics and security, technology, trade and connectivity, climate change, human security, democracy, governance, trust, spirituality and humanity.
CGS President Zillur Rahman and Executive Director Parvez Karim Abbasi delivered the welcome remarks at the opening of the conference.
Zillur Rahman said the Bay of Bengal is becoming increasingly important in the context of maritime security and regional geopolitics.
“As a vital link between South Asia and Southeast Asia, one of the key objectives of this initiative is to explore effective solutions to the challenges and opportunities rooted in the Bay,” he said.
He said this year’s discussions would focus on geopolitics, security, trust, climate change, spirituality and humanity.
The program includes public sessions such as plenaries, leadership forums and spotlight talks, as well as smaller invitation-only roundtables for in-depth discussions, according to the organisers.

item.title: UK maritime agency: Oil tankers attacked in Hormuz strait
item.description:
Two oil tankers have been struck by "unidentified projectiles" in the Strait of Hormuz region, a British maritime agency said Friday, in the latest threat to shipping in the waterway.
The Hormuz passage, through which a fifth of the world's oil and LNG passed before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February and sparked the Middle East war, remains at the heart of the conflict.
Tehran has been blocking the passage of commercial ships, firing on vessels it accuses of unauthorised crossings.
Washington responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting its oil.
The first attack caused "a small fire and blackout onboard", the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said Friday, adding that the fire was later extinguished.
There were no reported casualties or environmental impact, it added.
The vessel, which was exiting the strait, was able to resume its journey, UKMTO said, without specifying the ship's ports of origin and destination.
Hours later, another crude oil tanker reported being struck by an "unknown projectile" east of Oman, with all crew safe and no environmental damage reported, according to the UKMTO.
The agency said authorities were investigating the incidents.

item.title: Uranium consignment reaches Rooppur nuclear power plant amid tight security
item.description:
A uranium consignment for the second unit of Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant reached the project site in Pabna on Saturday afternoon amid tight security.
Three uranium-laden lorries arrived at the nuclear power plant site around 12:25pm after leaving Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at around 7:15am under the security escort of the Bangladesh Army, said Pabna Deputy Commissioner Aminul Islam.
The consignment is the first shipment of uranium for the second unit of the Rooppur plant.
A special cargo aircraft carrying the uranium landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at around 11:44pm on Friday.
After completing the necessary formalities, the uranium was transported to Rooppur in three lorries while another vehicle carried other equipment.
A team of specialists who had arrived from Russia also accompanied the consignment.
Members of the Bangladesh Army, police and various intelligence agencies were deployed to ensure security during the transportation.
The flight carrying uranium for Rooppur plant was scheduled to arrive on September 24 but was not given permission to use Pakistani airspace.
According to project officials, a total of nine uranium consignments are scheduled to be brought to Bangladesh — seven for the second unit and two for the refuelling of the first unit.
All the consignments are scheduled to be delivered by December.
Fuel for the first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was brought to Bangladesh in 2023.
The Rooppur plant, comprising two 1,200-megawatt units, has a total generation capacity of 2,400MW.
Construction of the plant began in 2013 with Russian assistance at an estimated cost of more than Tk1.13 lakh crore.
Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Ltd (NPCBL) Managing Director Dr Zahidul Hasan said testing of the 16-megawatt high-pressure system under the reactor protection and safety-related system was successfully completed on Wednesday following the replacement of a defective valve.

item.title: North Korea fires ballistic missile after Seoul’s apology demand
item.description:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile, Seoul’s military said Saturday, days after demanding an apology for a blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ that it blames on the North.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility for last month’s explosion inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) and called South Korea “despicable” on Friday, undercutting overtures by Seoul’s civilian leadership seeking a return to dialogue.
Early Saturday, “our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
“South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defense posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles,” it said, adding the missile flew more than 700 kilometers (435 miles).
Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command found that last month’s explosion inside the DMZ, the heavily mined buffer dividing the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice, was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South side of the border.
North Korea’s military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off following leader Kim Jong Un’s designation of South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy” in 2024.
The mines responsible for the blast, which left three soldiers wounded, were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang’s border fortification work, according to South Korea’s defense minister Kang Shin-chul.
South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” on Friday and once again denied Pyongyang was behind the blasts.
She ridiculed Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch” and said the military’s demand her country apologize was “quite ridiculous.”
Kim also warned Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast -- remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
Analysts said the launch would be viewed as a show of force in response to the South Korean government’s diplomatic efforts, effectively rejecting engagement.
“Seoul called for easing tensions, but Pyongyang answered by escalating them,” Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP.
“The message is that the North is pursuing... confrontation in response to goodwill,” he added.
South Korea’s defense minister said on Tuesday the military had “a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages” to respond to the DMZ incident, without providing further detail.
The South’s Unification Minister, Chung Dong-young, also proposed talks to address issues along the border to Pyongyang on Friday.

item.title: Dengue cases up 74%, deaths 27% from last year
item.description:
Dengue hospitalizations in Bangladesh have surged by nearly 74% compared with the same period last year, with the outbreak accelerating dramatically in September and showing little sign of easing in the first three days of October.
A total of 84,369 dengue patients were hospitalized between January 1 and October 3 this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Compared with 48,491 hospitalizations during the corresponding period last year, as cited in the data reviewed by Dhaka Tribune, this represents 35,878 additional patients, a year-on-year increase of about 74%.
Deaths have also risen substantially. The toll stood at 256 as of Saturday, against 202 by October 3 last year -- an increase of 54 deaths, or nearly 27%.
Behind the year-on-year jump is a steep deterioration since the beginning of the monsoon, culminating in September, when the country recorded by far its highest monthly caseload and death toll of 2026.
September alone accounted for 43,774 hospitalizations and 148 deaths, meaning more than half of all dengue patients hospitalized this year and nearly 58% of the fatalities were recorded in a single month.
And October has begun with little respite.
In just the first three days of the month, another 4,749 dengue patients were admitted to hospitals and 11 died, pushing the cumulative figures from 79,620 hospitalizations and 245 deaths at the end of September to 84,369 and 256 respectively.
The month-by-month figures illustrate how rapidly the outbreak has escalated.
In June, 2,907 dengue patients were hospitalized and 13 died. July saw admissions more than triple to 9,206, with 36 deaths.
The situation worsened sharply in August, when 20,536 patients were hospitalized and 43 died.
Then came September.
Hospitalizations more than doubled from August to 43,774, while deaths jumped from 43 to 148, more than three times the previous month’s toll.
The trajectory has continued into October.
In the latest 24-hour reporting period alone, six people died and another 1,608 were hospitalized across the country.
Two of the deaths occurred in Dhaka South City Corporation and two in Rajshahi division, while Khulna and Barisal divisions recorded one each.
Of the new patients, Chittagong recorded the highest number outside the capital with 319 admissions, followed by Khulna with 276 and Barisal with 215.
Hospitals in Dhaka North City Corporation admitted 171 patients and those in Dhaka South 223, while another 131 were admitted elsewhere in Dhaka division.
Rajshahi recorded 132 new patients, Mymensingh 79 and Rangpur 62.
As of Saturday, 5,631 dengue patients remained under treatment in hospitals across the country, while 78,482 of those admitted this year had been discharged.
Entomologist Prof Dr Kabirul Bashar said the continuing rise showed why mosquito-control programs cannot depend primarily on fogging or killing adult Aedes mosquitoes.
Killing adult mosquitoes provides only temporary relief if eggs and larvae remain in breeding sites, allowing another generation to emerge, he said.
Construction sites have become major breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes, according to Bashar, who stressed the need to hold building owners and construction companies accountable for eliminating stagnant water.
Effective control, he said, requires several measures to operate simultaneously, destroying larvae, removing stagnant water, managing the surrounding environment and maintaining public awareness.
Sporadic drives launched when dengue infections begin rising cannot deliver sustainable results, he warned.
Instead, mosquito control has to continue throughout the year, including during winter when Aedes prevalence is relatively low and authorities have a better opportunity to suppress mosquito populations before the next transmission season.
In practice, however, mosquito-control activities often become less intensive during that period, he said.
With the patient load rising, the government is also strengthening clinical preparedness outside major hospitals.
State Minister for Health Dr MA Muhit said 1,600 doctors across 40 districts were receiving specialized training in dengue clinical management.
Around 350 senior physicians had previously undergone training-of-trainers sessions and were now training other doctors across the districts.
Muhit said the objective was to improve clinical management so that patients did not die because of mistakes or shortcomings in treatment and to ensure that district and upazila-level doctors were prepared if hospital admissions continued to rise.
The pressure is already visible in hospitals. Recent reporting from Dhaka found dedicated dengue wards and corners at some facilities full, forcing patients to be accommodated elsewhere as the caseload increased.
At a dengue awareness program in Mugda on Saturday, State Minister Habibur Rashid Habib called for greater public participation alongside city corporation operations, urging residents to regularly remove stagnant water and keep their homes and surroundings clean.
Despite the intensified response, health authorities cannot say when the outbreak will begin to subside.
Md Halimur Rashid, director of the Disease Control Division at DGHS, said dengue-control activities were being pursued at the highest levels of government, but the disease remained heavily influenced by rainfall, temperature and other environmental conditions.
As a result, he said, authorities could not provide a fixed timeframe for bringing the situation under control.
Bangladesh is still well below the catastrophic levels recorded during the 2023 epidemic, when 321,179 people were hospitalized and 1,705 died, the worst dengue outbreak in the country’s recorded history.
But this year’s trajectory is moving sharply in the wrong direction.
By Saturday, hospitalizations were already 74% higher than at the same point last year, deaths were up by about 27%, and more than half of the year’s patients had been recorded in September alone.
With another 4,749 hospitalizations in the first three days of October, the surge has now carried into a new month.

item.title: Govt employees to get 3 months’ salary arrears with October pay, calculation starts tomorrow
item.description:
Government officials and employees will receive nearly three months’ salary arrears in one payment under the new pay structure. However, how much each person will receive will depend on their new pay fixation.

The process will begin tomorrow, Monday. The Finance Division of the Ministry of Finance has asked that the process be completed by 20 October, according to Finance Division sources.

The new salaries of government employees will be fixed through the pay fixation module of iBAS++. Employees will log into the portal and provide their employment-related information.

They will first have to enter their personal details, including their national identity card information, date of birth, current position and grade, date of joining the service and current basic salary. They will also have to cross-check information from their previous pay fixation.

How much will govt employees’ salaries increase in 3 phases?

The basic salary for each employee under the new structure will be determined through the pay fixation process. Arrears will be calculated based on the difference between the new and previous salaries and the effective date.

According to Finance Division sources, once pay fixation is completed, the government will pay three months’ arrears in a lump sum. However, the amount will not be the same for everyone. The amount of arrears will depend on the employee’s grade, current basic salary, salary fixed under the new structure and the date on which the new salary takes effect.

Employees who have received promotions, transfers, time scales, selection grades or higher grades will also have to provide those details. They will need to keep the relevant office orders and necessary documents ready as proof.

In particular, names, NID numbers, dates of birth, designations, grades and salary-related information should be checked carefully. Incorrect or incomplete information could create complications in the pay fixation process.

The mobile phone number registered with iBAS++ will be required. Those who do not have an NID will have to apply after updating their date of birth and other information recorded in their service documents.

After 11 years, the government issued a gazette notification on 19 September to implement a new national pay structure for government employees. Under the new structure, the minimum basic salary has been set at Tk 20,000 and the maximum at Tk 156,000.

Salaries and allowances will be provided in phases over the 2026–27 and 2027–28 financial years. The first phase of the basic salary will cover 1 July to 31 December 2026, the second phase 1 January to 30 June 2027, and the third phase 1 July to 31 December 2027. Allowances will take effect from 1 January 2028.

According to the gazette notification, salaries under the new structure will be fixed based on the basic salary as of 30 June 2026. Forty per cent of the difference between the new and old basic salaries will be paid from 1 July to 31 December this year.

From 1 January to 30 June 2027, 70 per cent of the difference will be paid. From 1 July 2027, the full new basic salary will take effect. According to Finance Division sources, Tk 370 billion has been allocated in the current financial year to pay 70 per cent of the basic salary difference in two instalments.

The new pay scale brings relief and risks

Accounts offices to verify information

After an employee submits their information online, the relevant accounts office will verify it. If any discrepancies are found between the information and supporting documents, corrections may be required.

In other words, simply filling in the information online will not complete the process. The new information must match the employee’s previous service history and pay fixation records. If employees face problems submitting information online, they will be able to seek assistance from the relevant accounts officer.

Once pay fixation is finalised salary bills will be prepared based on the new basic salary. At the same time, the amount of arrears due will also be finalised.

To ensure that pay fixation is completed smoothly, online training is being provided to officials of accounts offices. iBAS++ is providing the training under the Finance Division’s ‘Strengthening Public Financial Management to Enable Service Delivery’ programme (SPFMS).

Relevant officials and employees from the offices of the Chief Accounts and Finance Officer (CAFO), Divisional Controller of Accounts (DCA), District Accounts and Finance Officer (DAFO) and Upazila Accounts Officer (UAO) are taking part in the training.

New recruits to receive bigger pay rises, different calculation for existing employees

Complications over calculations under new structure

Under the new pay order, a permanent employee who completes eight years in the same post without promotion and whose service is satisfactory will receive the next higher grade. After receiving the first higher grade, they will be eligible for a second higher grade after completing another six years in the same post.

However, officials of the Finance Division say there are complications in calculating salaries under the new structure for employees who received a time scale, selection grade or higher grade under the previous pay structure. These issues are being resolved.

According to a Finance Division order, if an employee received two or more selection grades, time scales or higher grades in the same post under the previous pay structure, they will no longer be eligible for a higher grade in that post under the new pay structure.

On the other hand, if an employee had received only one higher scale or grade in the same post as of 30 June 2026, they will be eligible for a second higher grade after completing the next six years.

Finance Division sources say that during pay fixation from 5 to 20 October, employees’ previous promotions, higher grades and pay fixation history must be properly verified alongside their current salary. Only when these records are accurate will it be possible to correctly calculate the new salary and arrears due.

LPG 12kg cylinder price rises by Tk 252
item.description:
The price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplied by the private sector has increased at the consumer level. This time, the price has risen by Tk 21 per kilogramme.

As a result, the price of the most widely used 12kg LPG cylinder has increased by Tk 252, taking the new price to Tk 1,837 from Tk 1,585. The price had fallen by Tk 13 last month.

The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) announced the new price today, Sunday. The new price will take effect from 6:00 pm today. LPG prices rose in the wake of the outbreak of war in the Middle East.

LPG shortage as imports fall, prices rise

Following the start of a ceasefire, LPG prices began to decline on the international market. Prices had fluctuated over the past two months, but a significant surge has occurred again this month.

However, LPG supply in the market has remained below demand for the past three weeks. As a result, there have been allegations that 12kg LPG cylinders are being sold at Tk 500 to Tk 800 above the official price.

Earlier, LPG prices on the international market rose after the war spread across the Middle East. In April, the country recorded its highest-ever increase in LPG prices.

At the beginning of April, the price of a 12kg LPG cylinder was increased by Tk 387. It was raised by another Tk 212 on 19 April. However, prices fell for two consecutive months in June and July.

LPG import: BPC fails even after 7 months

According to BERC, LPG cylinders of various sizes are available in the market. From now on, the price of LPG will be Tk 153.06 per kilogramme. The prices of LPG cylinders of different sizes will be determined accordingly. Previously, the price was Tk 132.12 per kilogramme.

The commission determines LPG prices every month. However, LPG is not being sold in the market at the officially set prices. The 12kg LPG cylinder is the most widely used for household purposes.

There have been allegations that LPG sellers are charging customers more than the official price for each cylinder. Many people are turning to LPG cylinders for cooking at home amid the gas shortage.

The price of 12.5kg LPG cylinders supplied by state-owned companies has been kept unchanged at Tk 825. Meanwhile, the price of LPG used in vehicles, known as auto gas, has been set at Tk 84.62 per litre. Previously, it was Tk 73.09 per litre.

BERC has been setting LPG prices since April 2021. Propane and butane, the main components used to produce LPG, are imported from various countries. Every month, Saudi Arabian company Aramco publishes the prices of these two LPG components. This is known as the Saudi Contract Price (CP).

BERC adjusts LPG prices in Bangladesh based on this Saudi CP as the benchmark price. The commission calculates the average US dollar exchange rate for the entire month based on the invoice prices submitted by importing companies.

item.title: American Deisseroth, Germans Hegemann and Nagel win 2026 Nobel medicine prize for brain research
item.description:
SWEDEN-NOBEL-AWARD-MEDICINE-PHYSIOLOGY

Scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for "discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics," the award-giving body said on Monday.

Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden's Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners.

Optogenetics "makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain," the prize-givers said.

"This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries."

The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual Nobel announcements, with awards in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics to follow over the coming days.

The five original Nobel Prizes were created under the terms of Swedish inventor and industrialist Alfred Nobel's will and have been awarded since 1901, with only limited interruptions, chiefly during the World War One and World War Two.

A sixth award, the economics prize, was established in 1968 by Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank.

The medicine prize has honoured some of the most influential scientific discoveries of the past century, including Alexander Fleming's work on penicillin, recognised in 1945, and Karl Landsteiner, who won in 1930 for his discovery of human blood groups.

Last year, American scientists Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell and Japan's Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for work shedding light on how the immune system spares healthy cells, creating openings for possible new treatments of diseases such as cancer.

Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The awards are presented in Stockholm, with the exception of the Peace Prize, which is handed out in Oslo, a tradition often linked to the union that bound Sweden and Norway during Nobel's lifetime.

More than 125 years after Nobel signed his will, the prizes retain many of their longstanding traditions.

The celebrations culminate on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death, when laureates receive their awards in ceremonies attended by Sweden's and Norway's royal families and are feted at gala banquets held in their honour.

item.title: Turkey, Pakistan to deploy forces to Saudi amid Houthi attacks: joint statement
item.description:
SAUDI-TURKEY-PAKISTAN-DIPLOMACY-DEFENCE

Turkey and Pakistan will undertake a “rapid deployment” of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defence alliance, the three countries said Monday, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen’s Houthis.

The three countries in August signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event one were attacked.

The pact unites NATO’s second-largest army, that of Turkey, with the Islamic world’s only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the leading Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.

Their representatives held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday where they noted recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular ones targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Iran-backed Houthis by name.

The trio “reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom’s security and territorial integrity”, they said in a joint statement.

They also agreed “to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom”.

The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.

The kingdom has faced repeated Houthi attacks targeting its cities, oil infrastructure and ships ever since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.

In September, the group launched a new offensive that seized swathes of territory from Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which on Monday launched a counteroffensive with Riyadh’s support seeking to retake all Houthi territory, some of it held for more than a decade.

COP31 eyes modest steps as climate disasters multiply
item.description:
Nations reeling from a year of climate devastation gather for COP31 next month, but negotiations are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The conference follows deadly heatwaves and fires in Europe, catastrophic floods in Nepal and record temperatures around the world, testing whether the United Nations-backed talks can keep pace with reality.
As leaders meet in Turkey, an exceptionally powerful El Niño pattern will be approaching peak strength, threatening to amplify weather chaos worldwide and drive global heat to unprecedented highs.
Concerns over energy security will also loom large, with no end in sight to the Middle East war that has sent oil and gas prices soaring and hit fossil fuel-importing nations hard.
With a new agreement on fossil fuels unlikely, Turkey is rallying support for a voluntary "electrification" pledge it says could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on energy imports.
"In many ways, the defining contexts for this year's climate summit will be heat and Hormuz," said David Waskow from the World Resources Institute, referencing the vital strait that carried one-fifth of the world's hydrocarbons before the Iran war.
Unusually, Turkey must navigate these complexities with Australia, a major fossil fuel exporter, after both countries agreed to share COP31 duties following a bruising hosting battle.
Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations in Antalya starting November 9, said this year's extreme events "show climate change is not a future challenge".
"It is a present reality... and the costs of inaction are rising," he said.
A "pre-COP" meeting began Monday in the climate-vulnerable Pacific with a leaders' retreat in Tuvalu and government meetings in Fiji.
Unlike recent COPs -- where nearly 200 nations forged landmark pacts on phasing down coal or moving away from fossil fuels -- the negotiation agenda at COP31 is light on big-ticket items.
There are more than 100 items on the table but many deal with technical matters, like approving indicators to track progress on climate adaptation.
"Much of the Antalya summit will be a 'roll up the sleeves' effort. Governments need to make concrete headway in negotiations, though there may not be dramatic outcomes this year," Waskow told AFP.
Nations are not expected to adopt new binding commitments to reduce the burning of fossil fuels -- the leading cause of climate change.
Countries agreed in 2023 to move away from coal, oil and gas but since then efforts to negotiate concrete targets or timelines for that transition have gone nowhere.
At last year's summit, fossil fuels were not mentioned by name in the final agreement after oil and gas-producing nations prevented consensus on the issue.
"Everyone agrees there will be no real gain at the multilateral level at the moment," Marta Torres-Gunfaus from the IDDRI think tank told AFP.
Fossil fuel emissions, meanwhile, hit record highs in 2025.
In September, the UN conceded that the milestone 1.5C climate target will be missed in a matter of years.
Nations frustrated at the COP gridlock have sought progress elsewhere.
Nearly 60 countries attended a fossil fuel phaseout conference without UN involvement this year.
France, the Netherlands and Germany have published "roadmaps" with explicit deadlines for quitting coal, oil and gas.
UN Climate chief Simon Stiell has defended the negotiations while acknowledging their limitations: "No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward," he said.
Turkey says it is not realistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace.
"Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail," said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Turkey is curating an "action agenda" alongside the negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
There is broad support for its centrepiece goal: raising the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20% on Tuesday to 35% by 2035.
The electrification target does not state how that extra power should be produced. One-third of electricity is generated by coal, and there are concerns the target could provide cover for expanded fossil fuel use.
The Nepal floods would also put "a huge amount of pressure" on western countries to increase financial support for climate disaster recovery, said Ajay Mathur, a former Indian government negotiator.
"We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying for it," Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said.

Student protests rock French; police fire teargas, arrest 6,100
item.description:
FRANCE-PROTEST/

Police fired tear gas at protesters blockading French high schools on Tuesday as students, teachers and parents took to the streets on the biggest day of action in a wave of demonstrations against understaffed and dilapidated classrooms.

In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs marked with "The state has killed national education" and other messages, in largely peaceful rallies. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city.

But in Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes, the demonstrations at times turned violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.

"There is such a gap between the elites and us," said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg.

The protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris, before spreading nationwide, presenting a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron's cash-strapped government at a time when it faces strong economic headwinds.

The High School Students Union said more than half of France's high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online.

"We want more money for the national educational system so that high schools are renovated," said Roberta, another recent high-school graduate at a protest outside Paris' prestigious Henri IV school.

Schools were facing a list of problems from water leaks to rat infestations, she added.

Thousands of arrests

The government has responded to the demonstrations with riot police.

Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.

France's interior ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said, without specifying the crimes.

At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu's office.

A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday. The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade.

"They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters," said Omar Slaouti, a high school teacher in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris.

"If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake," he added.

Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and Le Pen's National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests. LFI denies the accusation.

Prime minister promises a response

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students' leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.

The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.

Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government's words were not enough. "That's all fine and dandy, but that's not what's going to change the daily lives of our children," she said.

Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult.

The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France's growing debt pile, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push bond yields higher. The yield on France's 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.

The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right euro-sceptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring's election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.

item.title: Latest attack on civil and political rights of Bangladesh citizens: HRW
item.description:
The mass arrest of attendees at a small left-wing party’s meeting in Dhaka on 26 September is the latest incident in the Bangladesh authorities’ ongoing assault on civil and political rights, according to a report run on the website of Human Rights Watch (HRW).

Police took around 290 supporters of the Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal into custody after members of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s youth wing – the Jubo Dal – claimed the gathering was a 'secret' meeting of the former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League, whose activities are currently banned.

A court remanded 27 of those arrested to custody, because it was alleged they had chanted the slogan 'Joy Bangla' (Victory to Bengal), a slogan associated with the Awami League.

The Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal was part of a 14-party alliance, led by the Awami League, that governed Bangladesh from 2009 until 2024, when it was toppled by student led protests in which hundreds were killed by security forces.

The current ruling party, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), faced severe repression under the Awami League government. Since being elected in February, it has targeted its own perceived opponents with arbitrary detention and hundreds of Awami League members are currently in jail, mostly without charge.

Police have repeatedly raided alleged gatherings of Awami League supporters.

On 26 September, the same day as the Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal meeting, police in Barisal detained 12 Awami League activists for allegedly holding a 'secret' meeting to 'plan sabotage', two days later, 15 were arrested in Dhaka under the Anti-Terrorism Act on similar allegations.

In both cases those detained said they had gathered to mark Sheikh Hasina’s birthday.

During Sheikh Hasina’s authoritarian rule, there were widespread and grave rights violations—including extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, torture and the arbitrary detention of political opponents.

The Bangladesh Nationalist Party came to power promising to restore human rights and the rule of law. Instead, the new government has arbitrarily detained perceived opponents and rolled back human rights safeguards the interim government proposed.

International human rights law guarantees freedoms of expression and association for all. Past violations of those rights committed when Awami League was in power cannot justify the Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s current violations of the same rights. Bangladeshi history is rife with examples of where such repression can lead.

item.title: PM Tarique to visit Japan, manpower deal on cards
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is set to visit Japan on October 26 for a four-day official trip, with Dhaka and Tokyo working to finalise a manpower agreement that could emerge as one of the key outcomes of his first bilateral visit to the country.
The October 26-29 visit will take place at the invitation of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, according to Foreign Ministry and diplomatic sources.
The two leaders are scheduled to hold bilateral talks in Tokyo, while Tarique is also expected to meet Emperor Naruhito.
The dates and planned visit were also reported by multiple diplomatic sources on Tuesday.
Officials said manpower exports, Japanese investment, trade and energy cooperation are expected to feature prominently in the talks, as the two countries seek to deepen their Strategic Partnership.
Several memorandums of understanding and agreements are being discussed ahead of the visit, diplomatic sources said.
Among them, an MoU related to sending Bangladeshi workers to Japan is at an advanced stage of negotiations and could be signed during the prime minister’s visit if the two sides reach final agreement.
The manpower issue gives the visit particular significance as Bangladesh seeks to expand access to Japan’s labour market amid Tokyo’s growing demand for foreign workers.
Japan announced last year that it planned to recruit at least 100,000 Bangladeshi workers over five years.
Bangladesh and Japan also signed two MoUs in Tokyo in May 2025 aimed at developing skilled manpower for the Japanese market.
Since then, Dhaka has sought to accelerate recruitment by expanding Japanese-language and technical training and addressing procedural barriers facing Bangladeshi workers.
The government has also established a dedicated Japan Cell under the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment.
The ministry says Bangladesh plans to send 100,000 workers to Japan annually in response to Japanese demand, with opportunities primarily under the Technical Intern Training Programme, Specified Skilled Worker scheme and professional employment categories.
Tarique himself has made expansion of the Japanese labour market a priority.
During a meeting with a special adviser to the Japanese prime minister in July, he urged Tokyo to recruit more skilled Bangladeshi workers and sought greater Japanese cooperation in skills development and investment.
The upcoming visit is therefore expected to review progress on those initiatives and explore ways to translate existing commitments into greater numbers of Bangladeshi workers entering Japan.
The invitation for Tarique to visit Japan was formally conveyed on behalf of Takaichi during recent high-level exchanges between the two governments.
The Japanese side reiterated the invitation during bilateral consultations, while Bangladesh invited Takaichi to visit Dhaka at a mutually convenient time.
Foreign Ministry officials said the two prime ministers would discuss ways to expand economic cooperation, with Bangladesh particularly interested in attracting further Japanese investment.
Japan is already one of Bangladesh’s major development partners and has been involved in large infrastructure projects, while the two countries have increasingly sought to move the relationship beyond traditional development assistance towards trade, investment, skills and strategic cooperation.

item.title: Belgium's Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize
item.description:
Belgian physicist Francis Halzen on Tuesday won the Nobel physics prize for groundbreaking work using South Pole ice to capture neutrinos originating in the distant cosmos, providing insight into the far reaches of space.
“This year’s prize is about ghostly messengers from space,” Ellen Moons, secretary general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a news conference.
Halzen was honored “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” the jury said.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said Halzen’s work had been fundamental for the observatory -- “a cubic kilometer of ice that is equipped with light sensors” -- and has “paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.”
Using the observatory, researchers can capture neutrinos -- rare subatomic particles -- “from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe.”
Halzen, 82, was born in Tienen, Belgium and is a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the United States, where he is a citizen.
“It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” he told the news conference by telephone shortly after the prize was announced.
“But it’s a great pleasure to hear about this prize,” Halzen said.
The academy explained that high energy neutrinos are created in the same environments as other particles.
“However, unlike other particles, neutrinos reach us without changing direction or losing energy. This means they can provide information that is not available in any other way,” it said in a statement.
Halzen first presented his idea for the observatory in 1988 and his idea quickly gained the support of other researchers.
Preliminary testing was conducted just a few years later but the observatory was not completed until 2011.
“Cosmic neutrinos with extremely high energies are very rare, so an enormous volume of ice is needed to observe an adequate number of collisions,” the jury explained.
“For me, the main pleasure of it, besides winning the Nobel Prize, is that I hope this reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project,” Halzen said.
The award is the second Nobel of the season, after the medicine prize was awarded on Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.
The researchers were honored for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics, which involves controlling nerve signals with light.
Last year, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to Briton John Clarke, Frenchman Michel Devoret and American John Martinis for putting quantum mechanics into action and enabling the development of all kinds of digital technology from cellphones to a new generation of computers.
The physics prize will be followed by the chemistry one on Wednesday.
The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.
The most keenly anticipated award -- the peace prize -- is due on Friday.
US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively last year to get the prize -- and Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado ended up giving him her Nobel medal -- and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.
The Nobel consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a 12-million-kronor ($1.2-million) prize sum, which is shared if there is more than one winner in a discipline.
The laureates will receive their prizes at a formal ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

WTO hikes global trade growth forecast, names Pakistan among nations gaining from disruptions amid ME conflict
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: The World Trade Organisation on Thursday sharply raised its global trade growth forecast for 2026 — with merchandise trade riding the AI boom — and concluded that some nations, including Pakistan, were actually benefiting from trade disruptions amid the ongoing Middle East conflict in some ways.

In its Global Trade Outlook Update 2026, the Geneva-based global trade watchdog said its economists had upgraded their forecasts for global merchandise trade volume growth to 3.9 per cent for 2026 and 4.1pc for 2027 — up from previous estimates of 1.9pc and 2.6pc, respectively, projected at the start of the US-Iran conflict in March.

The report said that despite the conflict, the global economy had remained resilient, reflecting a stronger-than-expected surge in AI-related capital investment and increased supplies of fuels and fertilisers from countries outside the Middle East.

While several countries faced fuel transport disruptions because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the redistribution of traffic was creating opportunities for various other economies, it said.

“For example, Pakistan’s exports of sea freight transport services rose by 73pc year-on-year in the first half of 2026, as its transport operators benefited from increased traffic,” the WTO said.

Vessel calls at major container terminals in Karachi were still 14pc higher year-on-year in July, it added.

Exports by the United States to the European Union continued to expand while exports to Asia and the Pacific decreased by 2pc in the second quarter.

At the same time, computer services exports by several smaller and emerging players expanded rapidly. In the second quarter, computer services exports from Malaysia rose by 34pc, those from Pakistan by 23pc and by 13pc in Brazil.

The WTO also noted that the rerouting of vessels and containers towards alternative ports and trans-shipment hubs had put pressure on capacity in South Asia, translating into higher charges. In July, the Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) introduced a congestion surcharge of $500 per container on shipments from Northern Europe to India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

“Longer waiting and transit times are increasing costs for carriers and traders, some of which may ultimately be passed on to consumers,” it said.

Stronger-than-expected growth reflects opposing forces

The report revised the forecast for commercial services trade volume growth in 2026 down to 3.3pc from the previous 4.8pc, as the conflict in the Middle East has depressed travel and tourism in the region and raised fuel input costs worldwide.

In 2027, growth rates in volume terms for merchandise and commercial services trade were expected to rise to 4.1pc and 6.4pc, respectively, but this outcome depended on a timely resolution of the Middle East conflict, according to the WTO.

Based on these projections, the volume of global goods and services trade was expected to grow by approximately 3.7pc in 2026 and 4.7pc in 2027, the organisation forecast.

The stronger-than-expected growth in merchandise trade reflects two opposing forces, according to the watchdog. On the one hand, the push from AI-related investment has increased demand for AI-enabling goods, which accounted for 47pc of global merchandise trade growth in value terms in the first half of 2026. On the other hand, reduced shipments of oil, natural gas and fertilisers have weighed on merchandise trade; for the ongoing year to date, the former has outweighed the latter, the WTO said.

It noted that while high commodity prices may persist as a result of bottlenecks constraining the flows of fuels and fertilisers, continued AI investment and the broader digitisation of the global economy were expected to keep merchandise trade growth above the rate of global GDP growth in 2027.

“AI investment and the Middle East conflict are also affecting the services trade outlook, but to different degrees. AI is lifting trade in computer and financial services. However, the impact of the conflict in the Middle East is prevailing in traditional services such as transport, tourism and construction,” it said.

Conversely, services trade growth is expected to remain below trend this year before rebounding in 2027. Asia and North America are expected to see their contributions decline, while those of Europe are expected to remain broadly stable, putting the region on track to account for over half of the growth in export services this year.

Meanwhile, the rest of the world was expected to make a negative contribution, dragged down by a large contraction in the Middle East, the report added. All services sub-sectors are expected to see growth below the March baseline forecast.

However, it noted that the trade forecast remains subject to several significant risks.

“The current wedge between crude oil and refined oil prices is weighing on trade growth by eroding households’ purchasing power. A slowdown or reversal of AI investment spending could also have a significant impact on trade given its high import content,” it said.

Turning to trade statistics in value terms, the WTO said the current US dollar value of world merchandise trade had risen considerably faster than volume in the first half of 2026, up 15pc year-on-year compared to 3.5pc growth in volume terms.

“This marks one of the largest gaps between the value and volume of trade growth in recent years, reflecting higher prices for fuels and electronic components for data centres,” it said.

It noted that trade continued to show “some alignment with geopolitical considerations”, although it pointed out that the gap between intra-bloc and inter-bloc trade had narrowed through 2025 and into 2026, suggesting that “the broader pattern of bloc-based fragmentation has not continued to intensify”.

US-China trade decoupling had, however, accelerated since 2025 and was now the main driver of the bloc divergence, it added.

UNHRC adopts first-ever resolution on AI; Bangladesh acts as penholder
item.description:
The United Nations Human Rights Council has adopted by consensus the first-ever resolution on artificial intelligence (AI), titled “Implications of Artificial Intelligence for the Promotion and Protection of Human Rights”, with Bangladesh serving as the penholder and playing a leading role in advancing the initiative.
During the ongoing 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council, Bangladesh joined fellow Core Group members Algeria, Austria, Egypt, Greece, Guyana, Kuwait and Nepal in steering the initiative on AI and human rights.
Guided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh, the initiative was first presented before the Council in August 2026 by former Ambassador and Permanent Representative Nahida Sobhan on behalf of the Core Group.
Since then, the Core Group has pursued an open, inclusive and constructive process of engagement with Member States and relevant stakeholders.
The consensus adoption marks a significant step forward in strengthening the Council’s consideration of the evolving relationship between artificial intelligence and human rights, while keeping human dignity, development, inclusion and international cooperation at the centre.
It also reflects Bangladesh’s growing and constructive role in shaping international discussions at the intersection of emerging technologies, development and human rights, and its growing contribution to multilateral diplomacy.
Bangladesh underscored that continued constructive engagement and cooperation among Member States and stakeholders will remain essential as the initiative moves forward.

ECNEC approves 13 projects involving Tk 162 billion
item.description:
The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) today approved 13 projects involving total cost of Tk 162 billion, including a project to construct a 442-MW peak solar power plant at Rampal in Bagerhat.

Of the total project cost, Tk 106 billion will come from government funds, Tk 40.8 billion from project loans and Tk 15.2 billion from concerned agencies’ own funds.

The approval came at the 5th meeting of the ECNEC held at Bangladesh Secretariat with Prime Minister and ECNEC Chairman Tarique Rahman in the chair.

Of the approved 13 projects, 10 are new, two are revised and one involves extension of its implementation period.

State Minister for Planning Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki briefed reporters after the meeting at the NEC Conference Room in the city’s Sher-e-Bangla Nagar area.

Under the Tk 24.9 billion Rampal project, a 442-megawatt peak (MWp) solar power plant will be constructed at Rampal in Bagerhat, aimed at increasing renewable energy generation, diversifying the country’s primary fuel sources and reducing carbon emissions.

The Rampal 442 MWp Solar Power Plant Construction Project was proposed by the Power Division and will be implemented by the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB). The project will be financed by BPDB from its own with Tk 3.74 billion and from Power Sector Development Fund Tk 21.23 billion.

The Power Sector Development Fund loan would carry a 2 per cent interest rate, with a one-year grace period and a 16-year repayment period.
The Planning Commission recommended that the project be implemented from September 2026 to March 2029.

In its assessment, the Planning Commission said the project would increase renewable-energy-based electricity generation and contribute to the government’s target of raising renewable energy’s share of the total energy mix to 20 per cent by 2030.

Once the project is implemented, it would add 442 MW of electricity to the national grid. Currently the solar power generation in the country is 797 MW out of the total ongrid power generation capacity of 28,827 MW.

“The project will increase electricity generation based on renewable energy, which will help achieve the target of generating 20 per cent of electricity from renewable sources by 2030,” said the Planning Commission official.

The Planning Commission said the project would strengthen energy security by diversifying primary fuel sources and reduce carbon emissions.
The proposed plant will be built on 918.50 acres of land in Block-B of Rampal that BPDB had already acquired. The Planning Commission said the use of BPDB-owned land would eliminate the need for fresh land acquisition and reduce project costs.

Electricity generated by the solar plant will be transmitted through the existing transmission infrastructure associated with the nearby Rampal coal-fired power plant. The project summary said this would allow the plant to be implemented relatively quickly and at lower cost.

BPDB acquired a total of 1,834 acres in Rampal in 2012 for development of a coal-fired power plant. The land was divided into Block-A, covering 915.50 acres, and Block-B covering 918.50 acres.

Bangladesh-India Friendship Power Company (Pvt) Ltd’s Maitree Super Thermal Power Plant was built in Block-A, while Block-B remains under BPDB.

Land development and boundary-wall construction have already been completed in Block-B, according to the project document.

The proposed solar plant will use solar photovoltaic modules with a minimum capacity of 640 watts peak. The project will also install grid-tied inverters with a cumulative capacity of 360 MW, a pooling substation, a three-kilometre double-circuit 230-kV transmission line and three 230-kV bays, including one spare bay.

The largest component of the project cost, Tk 12.38 billion, or around 50 per cent, will go to solar photovoltaic modules and mounting structures.
Electrical equipment, including inverters, transformers and SCADA systems will cost Tk 7.32 billion.

The project summary said a feasibility study was conducted by the Infrastructure Investment Facilitation Company (IIFC) and found the project acceptable.

The project was included in the Annual Development Programme (ADP) for fiscal 2026-27 as an unapproved “green page” project.

The project is also aligned with the Five Year Strategic Framework for Reform and Development and the Sustainable Development Goal 7, which seeks to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all.

The day’s meeting also approved seven projects under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives.

The projects are - improving road infrastructure and drainage in 18 wards under five newly incorporated regions of Dhaka South City Corporation; upgrading important infrastructure in Rangpur City Corporation; rehabilitating damaged roads in Rangpur City Corporation, and constructing roads, drains and footpaths in zones one to eight of Gazipur City Corporation.

The other projects under the ministry include a project for women’s skills development and entrepreneurship creation through cooperatives; rural infrastructure development in Sirajganj, Bogura and Naogaon districts; and the Important Urban Infrastructure Development Project (2nd phase), which was approved in its second revised form.

The ECNEC also approved the third revised project for procuring 35 commercial and eight auxiliary vessels for Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Corporation (BIWTC) and constructing two new slipways under the Ministry of Shipping.

Under the Ministry of Railways, the committee approved the Railway Capacity Expansion Project for procuring 30 metre-gauge diesel-electric locomotives for Bangladesh Railway.

It also approved a project under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to renovate and modernise the purchased chancery building in Paris, France, to make it suitable for use.

Two projects under the Ministry of Road Transport and Bridges also received approval. One involves constructing the Second Karatoya Bridge at the 15th kilometre of the Bhajanpur (Nijbari)-Atorkhari-Mainaguri-Amtali-Mirgachh-Panchagarh (Z-5060) road.

The other is the second revised Thanchi-Rimakri-Madak-Likri Road Construction Project.

Meanwhile, the ECNEC meeting was informed about a project costing less than Tk 500 million that had already received approval from the Planning Minister.

The project involves re-excavating the Nandahar and Harabati rivers and Nunogola and Kharowa canals in Joypurhat district.

Ministers and State Ministers concerned attended the meeting while Planning Commission members and secretaries concerned were present.

French-Japanese duo wins Nobel for solving chemical asymmetry puzzle
item.description:
France’s Henri Kagan and Japan’s Kenso Soai on Wednesday won the Nobel chemistry prize for solving the mystery of why only one version of some molecules’ mirror-image forms appears in nature, a discovery decisive for the development of pharmaceuticals.
The pair were honored “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis,” the jury said.
Like hands, all amino acids exist as two mirrored variants, but only one of them is found in the proteins in the body’s cells.
The other is rarely found in nature, a phenomenon known as “homochirality,” the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained.
Chemists have long wondered how that process occurs, and the two Nobel laureates’ discoveries have “enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality,” the jury said.
“Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular,” said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
“Their discoveries have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals,” the jury said.
Last year, the chemistry prize went to Japan’s Susumu Kitagawa, UK-born Richard Robson and American-Jordanian Omar Yaghi for developing a method of designing molecular structures.
The chemistry prize follows the physics prize, which on Tuesday honored Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for groundbreaking work using Antarctic ice to capture particles originating in the distant cosmos.
On Monday, the medicine prize was awarded to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.
The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a prize for a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.
The most keenly anticipated award -- the peace prize -- is due on Friday.
US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively last year to get the prize and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.
The Nobel consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2-million prize sum, which is shared if there is more than one winner in a discipline.
The laureates will receive their prizes at a formal ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.
